876.title: Rattan Singh Bhangu
876.hook: his Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse
876.howItsDone: Rattan Singh Bhangu's Panth Prakash is read by Sikh historians and drawn on in gurdwara katha about the eighteenth century, alongside other sources.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how we know this: Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory. Your line was how do we know. Did you ask your elder? Today, one of those chroniclers, by name. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

A Sikh sits down to write. Not in prose. In verse, line after line that can be read aloud and remembered. He has the stories his family told him, the stories of the riders and the forests, the great killing, the temple blown up and rebuilt. Some of them are about his own family. And, by his own account, he has a reason to write: outsiders are asking about the Sikhs, and he wants the Sikh side told by a Sikh. Today: Rattan Singh Bhangu.
screen: `A SIKH WRITES IN VERSE.` → `STORIES HIS FAMILY TOLD HIM.` → `THE SIKH SIDE, TOLD BY A SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. It's called Panth Prakash. Panth is the path, and the word Sikhs use for the whole community. Prakash is light, the shining of something into view. So the title promises to bring the Panth into the light. Second, why he wrote it. Bhangu says that a British officer was collecting accounts of Sikh history, and that he heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them. So he set out to tell it from inside. That's a choice worth noticing. He didn't write an angry reply. He wrote the long story, with names, places and family memory, so it would be there for anyone who asked. Third, his family is in it. Bhangu traces his line to Mehtab Singh, one of the riders remembered for punishing the man who had turned the Harmandir into a place of drinking and dancing. So when he tells the hard century, he isn't telling strangers' stories. He's telling his own family's world. Fourth, how to read him. Because he wrote later, from memory and family tradition, historians read him carefully, setting him beside other sources. That's yesterday's lesson in action. And yet several stories on this path in recent weeks, Kapur Singh fanning the sangat, the boy Jassa Singh singing, the thirty at the Harmandir, are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his. When this path says tradition says, Bhangu is one of the voices in that tradition. The chronicler.
screen: `PANTH PRAKASH: THE PATH BROUGHT TO LIGHT.` · `WRITTEN SO THE SIKH SIDE WAS TOLD.` · `HIS OWN FAMILY IN THE STORY.` · `READ CAREFULLY, AND STILL TREASURED.` · then, large: `THE CHRONICLER.`

segments.voice: For this sit, read one line of history. It can be anything: a sentence from a history book, a plaque on a building, an inscription on a gravestone, an old letter, the first line of a page about where your family came from. Find it now, or recall one you know. Read it slowly, once. Then put it down and breathe. Ask: who wrote this, and from where were they standing? Let the question sit with you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhangu. The Sikh chronicler whose Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse, from family memory, so the Sikh side would be told. Today's word.
Your line: the chronicler. Today, write down one family story you've heard, just a few lines, with who told it to you, so it's there for someone who asks. Day eight hundred seventy-six.

877.title: Remembering without hatred
877.hook: the Ardas names martyrs, not enemies; memory is for courage, not revenge
877.howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas at the close of services and daily prayers; one passage remembers the martyrs by what they endured, the congregation answers Waheguru, and the prayer closes asking for the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rattan Singh Bhangu, who set the hard century down in verse. Your line was the chronicler. Whose story did you write down, or wish you had? Today, what Sikhs do with all that memory. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

Partway through the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings, there's a passage that's hard to hear. It remembers Sikhs who were cut limb from limb. Sikhs whose scalps were taken. Sikhs broken on the wheel, sawn apart, who gave their heads and kept their faith. The congregation stands with folded hands and answers Waheguru after it. And then something is missing. Listen for the names of the governors, the generals, the invaders who did these things. They aren't there. Today: remembering without hatred.
screen: `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` → `CUT, SCALPED, BROKEN, SAWN.` → `AND NOT ONE ENEMY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Start with what the prayer keeps. The Ardas names the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Piare, and then the ones whose names are lost, by what they endured and what they held on to. Their hair, their faith, their Guru. The focus is on the ones who stood, not on the ones who struck. That's the first thing. Memory pointed at courage. The second thing is the line Guru Arjan left in the Guru Granth Sahib, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. That's a hymn from a Guru who was himself put to death, and it can be heard alongside the long list of martyrs. It doesn't say nothing bad happened. It says the heart doesn't have to be organized around the people who did it. The third thing is how the prayer ends. After all that suffering, the Ardas closes by asking for the good of all, sarbat da bhala. Everyone. Not everyone except them. The same prayer that remembers the wheel and the saw asks for the well-being of the whole world. And this connects to something the path met a few weeks back: a minister whose grief turned into a slaughter. Sikhs tell that story too. Read this way, the Ardas keeps grief from being handed on as hatred. So when Sikhs stand and remember, the prayer doesn't ask who to pay back. It asks, in effect, could I stand like that? Courage, not revenge.
screen: `THE PRAYER NAMES THOSE WHO STOOD.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY, NO ONE A STRANGER.` · `IT ENDS ASKING THE GOOD OF ALL.` · `HATRED IS NOT HANDED ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE, NOT REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to remember without anger. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who went through something hard, in your family or your own life. Let yourself see it plainly. Now notice where your attention goes. If it keeps drifting to the person who caused it, gently bring it back to the one who endured. What did they hold on to? How did they stand? Stay there. If anger rises, let it pass through like weather, and come back. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings. It names the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all. Today's word.
Your line: courage, not revenge. Today, when an old hurt comes up, steer the story toward who stood up, not who knocked you down. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

878.title: The Budha Dal today
878.hook: the Nihang army traces itself to the elders' Dal of this century
878.howItsDone: Nihang Sikhs live in Dals with their own leaders and moving camps, wear blue with high turbans, keep horses and practice gatka, and gather for Hola Mohalla at Anandpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remembering without hatred: the Ardas names the martyrs, not the enemies, and asks the good of all. Your line was courage, not revenge. Where did you turn an old story toward who stood? Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

Deep blue robes. A turban wound high, almost a tower, ringed with steel circles and small blades. A spear in hand, a horse nearby, and a voice calling out the Khalsa's victory cry. If you've seen photographs from the festival of Hola Mohalla at Anandpur, you may have seen them: the Nihangs. They can look like figures stepped out of an old painting. They aren't a reenactment. They say they are the same army that rode through the century you've been hearing about, still riding. Today: the Budha Dal today.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, A TOWERING TURBAN.` → `HOLA MOHALLA AT ANANDPUR.` → `THE SAME ARMY, STILL RIDING.`

segments.voice: Go back a few weeks on this path. The Khalsa organized its riders into two bodies: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Budha means old. The elders' Dal kept the camps, guarded the shrines, held the memory. That's where today starts. The Nihang groups of today trace themselves to that body. One of them still carries the name Budha Dal and has its own jathedar, its own leader, and its own camps that move from place to place. In their telling, the line was never broken. The second thing is what they keep. Tradition says the Nihangs hold on to ways of the old riders that ordinary life elsewhere has left behind: the blue dress, the high turban with its weapons, life in moving camps, care for horses, the martial art called gatka, and a coded, joking way of speaking that belongs to the camps. To spend time with them is to see the hard century as a practice, not a chapter. The third thing is honest complexity. There's more than one Nihang Dal today, and they don't all agree, with each other or with other Sikhs, about every practice. Sikhs hold a range of views about them. What's clear is the claim they make: that the riders of the hard century didn't only leave descendants and stories. They left an army that still keeps its camp. The old army lives.
screen: `BUDHA DAL: THE ARMY OF THE ELDERS.` · `NIHANGS TRACE THEMSELVES TO IT.` · `BLUE DRESS, GATKA, MOVING CAMPS.` · `MORE THAN ONE DAL, MORE THAN ONE VIEW.` · then, large: `THE OLD ARMY LIVES.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with something living. Settle, and breathe. Bring up a tradition you've seen kept alive by real people: a recipe your grandmother still makes the old way, a song only sung at weddings, a craft somebody in your town still does by hand. Picture the person keeping it. Notice how much effort it takes, and how easily it could have stopped with them. Let yourself be a little grateful that it didn't. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Nihang. The order of Sikh warriors who say they are the elders' army of the hard century still riding: blue robes, high turbans, moving camps. Today's word.
Your line: the old army lives. Today, notice one old way that someone near you still keeps, and ask them about it. Day eight hundred seventy-eight.

879.title: Daily life on horseback
879.hook: cooking, praying and reading the Granth in camps
879.howItsDone: Sikhs say their daily prayers, the nitnem, morning, evening and night, often from memory or a small prayer book, wherever they are; at home, travel or work, the practice goes with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Budha Dal today: Nihang Sikhs who say the elders' army never broke camp. Your line was the old army lives. What old way did you notice someone keeping? Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

Before dawn in a riders' camp. Horses stamping in the cold. Somebody blowing on last night's coals. Nobody knows yet whether today means a long ride, a fight, or a day of hiding in tall grass. And before any of that is decided, voices start up, low, here and there among the tents and blankets: the morning prayers, said from memory. History books of this century fill up with battles and sieges. Today is about the hours in between. Today: daily life on horseback.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN IN A RIDERS' CAMP.` → `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DAY HOLDS.` → `THE MORNING PRAYERS, FROM MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Start with the prayers, because tradition puts them first. Guru Ram Das left a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib about what a Sikh's day looks like. Here in paraphrase: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes, and remembers the Name, and keeps remembering it sitting and standing through the day. Notice what that hymn needs. No building. No fixed address. Water and a voice. The riders could carry it anywhere, and tradition says they knew the daily prayers by heart. The second thing is the Granth itself. Tradition says the bands carried copies of the scripture with them, wrapped, and kept with care, and that when the camp stopped, a place was made for it and it was opened and read, the way it is in a gurdwara. A gurdwara, in a sense, could be pitched like a tent. The third thing is the food. Riders cooked what they could get: coarse bread, roasted grain, whatever a village shared. Tradition says even here the cooking was done together, and eaten together, sitting on the ground. Put the three side by side and a picture comes out. The hunted years didn't stop Sikh practice. They made it portable. The prayers lived in memory, the scripture in a bundle, the shared meal around whatever fire there was. And when the camp moved, all of it moved with it. Prayer on the move.
screen: `RISE EARLY, REMEMBER THE NAME.` · `THE PRAYERS CARRIED BY HEART.` · `THE GRANTH OPENED WHEREVER THEY STOPPED.` · `COOKED TOGETHER, EATEN ON THE GROUND.` · then, large: `PRAYER ON THE MOVE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes somewhere new. If you can, move. Stand up and go to a different spot: the step outside the door, a different chair, the floor by a window, even the car before you start it. If you can't move, turn to face a different wall. Settle there, and breathe. Notice how the place is different and how the practice is the same. Whatever you usually do, a breath, a line of prayer, silence, do it here. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Granth, the scripture the hunted riders carried wrapped and opened wherever the camp stopped. In the riders' camps, prayers said from memory, and food cooked and eaten together. Today's word.
Your line: prayer on the move. Today, take your practice somewhere it's never been: a bus, a walk, a waiting room. See if it travels. Day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: Langar in hard times
880.hook: even hunted, the camps kept a shared kitchen
880.howItsDone: Gurdwaras keep langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor; Sikhs give food, money and time to keep it running.

segments.voice: Yesterday, daily life on horseback: prayers by heart, the Granth opened wherever the camp stopped. Your line was prayer on the move. Where did your practice travel? Today, the pot over the fire. Day eight hundred eighty.

Rice cooked sweet with ghee, and a woman sharing it out to whoever sits down. That scene is in the Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad by the musicians Satta and Balwand. The woman is Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife, and the place is the Guru's langar, the free kitchen. Generations later, the Khalsa was hunted through forests and marshes, with little flour to spare. So what happened to that kitchen? Today: langar in hard times.
screen: `SWEET RICE IN THE GURU'S KITCHEN.` → `MATA KHIVI IN THE SCRIPTURE.` → `THEN THE HUNTED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Begin with the ballad, because the Guru Granth Sahib itself remembers the kitchen. Here in paraphrase: Mata Khivi is a good woman whose shade is thick like a leafy tree, and in the Guru's langar, rich sweet rice is shared out. A woman feeding people made it into the scripture. That's the first thing. The kitchen is holy ground. The second thing is the hard century. Tradition says that even when the Khalsa was hunted, living in forests and moving at night, the bands kept a common pot. When there was little, the little was divided. And the old teaching held: anyone who came to the fire, Sikh or not, stranger or not, was fed. Ten days ago, on the coins struck at Lahore, you heard three words, deg, tegh, fateh: the pot, the sword, victory, with the pot first. In the camps that order was a daily habit, not a slogan. A band that couldn't protect its own village for a season could still share its bread. The third thing is the people around them. Tradition says villagers who gave grain to the riders were fed from the same pot. In the stories, the kitchen was how the Khalsa stayed a people and not just an army. Here's the part worth repeating tonight. Langar was never only charity, the rich feeding the poor. In the hard century the cooks were poor too. They shared anyway. That's the shape of it on an ordinary day as well: not waiting until there's plenty, but setting out what there is. Share it anyway.
screen: `THE KITCHEN IS HOLY GROUND.` · `A COMMON POT, EVEN HUNTED.` · `ANYONE AT THE FIRE WAS FED.` · `THE COOKS WERE POOR TOO.` · then, large: `SHARE IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with what you have. Settle, and breathe. Think about your food today: what's in the fridge, the snack in your bag, the lunch you're planning. Not what you'd give if you had more. What's actually there. Now picture one person you could share a piece of it with: a coworker, a neighbor, a kid, someone at the door. Picture handing it over. Notice whether something in you clenches, and let it loosen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
langar, the Guru's free kitchen, kept going even when hunted: a common pot, feeding whoever came, with deg, the cooking pot, before the sword. Today's word.
Your line: share it anyway. Today, split something you'd normally keep for yourself, even if it's small, even if it's the last one. Day eight hundred eighty.

881.title: The Khalsa shall rule
881.hook: a couplet after Ardas speaks of the Khalsa ruling; Sikhs understand it in several ways, from justice to spiritual sovereignty
881.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the congregation often sings the couplet beginning raj karega Khalsa after the Ardas, standing, and Sikh teachers explain it as sovereignty, as just and gentle rule, and as mastery of the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar in hard times: deg, the cooking pot, before the sword. Your line was share it anyway. What did you split that you'd usually keep? Day eight hundred eighty-one.

The Ardas is over. The congregation is still standing, hands folded. And then the whole room sings a short couplet together, loud and steady. It opens with three words in Punjabi: raj karega Khalsa. The Khalsa shall rule. For a visitor hearing it for the first time, it can land with a jolt. Rule over whom? Rule how? Those are fair questions, and Sikhs themselves answer them in more than one way. Today: the Khalsa shall rule.
screen: `AFTER THE ARDAS, A SUNG COUPLET.` → `RAJ KAREGA KHALSA.` → `RULE OVER WHOM? RULE HOW?`

segments.voice: Start with where it comes from. The couplet isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition attributes it to Guru Gobind Singh, and it's recorded in one of the old codes of Sikh conduct. Its next lines say, in paraphrase, that none will stay defiant, that the ones who wandered in misery will come together, and that those who take shelter will be safe. Tradition says it was sung through the hunted century by people with a price on their heads. That's the first way Sikhs hear it: a promise of sovereignty, said aloud at the very moment it looked impossible, and later remembered when Sikh chiefs did hold the land. The second way is justice. Guru Arjan, in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes the kind of rule he means. Here in paraphrase: by the merciful one's command, no one pushes another around, no one hurts another, and everyone lives at ease. He calls it halemi raj, a gentle rule. Some readers hear raj karega Khalsa through that line: a rule where nobody is crushed. The third way turns inward. Khalsa can mean the pure, those who belong directly to the Guru. In this reading, the first kingdom to be ruled is the self: anger, greed, ego, fear. A person who can't rule their own temper isn't ready to rule anything else. These readings don't cancel each other out. Sikhs hold them side by side, and different gurdwaras and teachers lean different ways. But the third one is the one anyone can try on today. Rule yourself first.
screen: `A PROMISE SUNG WHILE HUNTED.` · `HALEMI RAJ: A GENTLE RULE.` · `THE FIRST KINGDOM IS THE SELF.` · `READINGS HELD SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RULE YOURSELF FIRST.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in your own small kingdom. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one plain question: what in me tends to take over? Maybe it's temper in traffic, the phone at midnight, the urge to win every argument, worry that runs the whole morning. Name just one. Then picture the next time it rises, and picture yourself, for one breath, choosing what happens next. Not crushing it. Just being the one in charge. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

halemi raj, the gentle rule Guru Arjan describes, where no one pushes another around and everyone lives at ease. Sikhs hear it in the couplet sung after the Ardas, alongside sovereignty and ruling one's own self. Today's word.
Your line: rule yourself first. Today, when the thing you named starts to take over, take one breath and make the next move yours. Day eight hundred eighty-one.

882.title: Visiting the sites
882.hook: gurdwaras now mark Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira
882.howItsDone: Gurdwaras stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira; Sikhs visit to pray and remember the two ghallugharas, and the anniversaries are marked there with readings, kirtan and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Khalsa shall rule: a couplet heard as sovereignty, as halemi raj the gentle rule, and as ruling the self. Your line was rule yourself first. What did you take charge of? Day eight hundred eighty-two.

Flat fields. Wheat, or mustard in its season, running to the edge of sight. An irrigation channel, a dirt road, a tractor parked by a wall. And in the middle of it, a white building with a dome and a tall flagpole, the saffron Nishan Sahib lifting in the wind. If you didn't know the story, you'd see a village gurdwara like any other. But this ground has a name in Sikh memory. Two places like this are where today goes. Today: visiting the sites.
screen: `FLAT FIELDS, A DIRT ROAD.` → `A WHITE DOME, A SAFFRON FLAG.` → `GROUND WITH A NAME IN MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The first place is Kahnuwan, near the marshes where, a few weeks back on this path, the families and riders were trapped in the smaller holocaust, the chhota ghallughara. Ghallughara means a great destruction. Chhota means small, though nothing about it was small to the people who lived it. Today a gurdwara stands there, and Sikhs come to remember. The second place is Kup Rahira, where the Khalsa made a moving ring around its families and the great holocaust, the vadda ghallughara, fell on them. A gurdwara marks that ground too. Those are the two facts. Now the meaning. Notice what stands at the heart of each site. Not a battle trophy. Not a wall of grievance. A gurdwara: a place where the Guru Granth Sahib is opened, hymns are sung, and a langar feeds anyone who walks in. The memorial is a working kitchen. That fits everything this week has been about: memory pointed at courage, the pot before the sword. And there's a quiet lesson in the sites themselves. The fields came back. Crops grow right up to the gurdwara walls. A child can grow up within sight of the gurdwara and learn the story from the person who serves them tea there. The places hold what happened so that the people who live there don't have to carry it alone. This week: Rattan Singh Bhangu, remembering without hatred, the Budha Dal today, daily life on horseback, langar in hard times, the Khalsa shall rule, and visiting the sites. The places remember.
screen: `KAHNUWAN: THE SMALLER HOLOCAUST.` · `KUP RAHIRA: THE GREAT HOLOCAUST.` · `NOT A MONUMENT, A GURDWARA.` · `THE FIELDS CAME BACK.` · then, large: `THE PLACES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a map. If you have a phone nearby, open a map and search for Kahnuwan, or Kup Rahira. Don't read anything. Just find it. Zoom in until you can see the fields, the roads, the shape of the village. Then put the phone down, close your eyes, and breathe. Hold the picture of that ordinary ground and what tradition says happened there. If you can't look it up, hold the picture of the white dome in the fields. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
ghallughara, the great destruction; gurdwaras now stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira, where the two ghallugharas fell, with scripture, song and a kitchen. Today's word.

original.note: Gurmukhi for ghallughara, a great destruction, the word Sikhs use for the two holocausts.

trapdoor: what you thought: old battlefields are fenced off and silent.
what it means: at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira, gurdwaras stand in working fields, with scripture, song and langar.
what a scholar hears: Sikh memory marks its sites of suffering with living gurdwaras, so remembrance happens through worship and a shared meal at the center, not only a battle monument.
